title: Living With Mom and Dad at Age 33
author: Aaron Renn
summary: A Wall Street Journal article about young adults living at home provides the launching point for a broader analysis of delayed adulthood, social belonging, and the fragmentation of civic life in America. By July 2020, 52% of young Americans aged 18–29 lived with at least one parent — the highest rate since the Great Depression — and the stigma around this arrangement is declining, with some young adults actively broadcasting the choice on social media. The author sees this as part of a wider failure-to-launch pattern driven by housing costs, declining civic institutions, and the erosion of 'ambient belonging' — the degree to which an environment lowers social friction between people. Jeff Giesea's concept of ambient belonging, developed after walking the Camino de Santiago, identifies the structural conditions that make connection easy or hard, rather than treating loneliness as a personal failing. Money increasingly determines access to ambient belonging through private clubs and exclusive spaces, widening the K-shaped divide in social life.
points: By July 2020, 52% of Americans aged 18–29 lived with at least one parent — the highest share since the Great Depression — and social stigma around the arrangement is declining significantly.

Adult children living at home reflects a broader failure-to-launch pattern driven by housing costs, declining real wages, and the disappearance of the civic infrastructure that once made independent adult life more viable.

Ambient belonging — the degree to which an environment lowers social friction between people — is a structural condition, not a personal trait; belonging is a design question, not just a psychological one.

As civic life has declined and public spaces have degraded, money plays two roles: it lets people buy insulation from negative environments, and it lets them buy into privatized ambient belonging via private clubs.
Boomers are increasingly upsizing rather than downsizing their homes, occupying the best school districts and displacing young families, compounding the housing pressures facing the next generation.
quotes: By July 2020, 52% of young Americans age 18 to 29 lived with at least one parent, according to a Pew Research Center analysis of census data. It was the first time a majority of young adults in the country had lived with parents since the Great Depression.
Living at home is in line with other trends showing a failure to launch among younger people, or greater delays in achieving the markers of traditional adulthood.
Young people say that living at home in 2026 doesn’t carry the stigma it once did because of how unaffordable life has become

Ambient belonging is the degree to which an environment lowers social friction between people. It’s not the thick, durable belonging we find in family, lifelong friends, or close-knit communities. It’s a social atmosphere where membership is presumed and connection requires less effort.

Money cuts both ways. It can buy us out of ambient belonging through McMansions, remote work, private rooms, and frictionless convenience. But it can also buy us access to it through private clubs, schools, camps, churches, and experiences that create repeated contact and shared identity.
As civic life has declined, trust has eroded in our society, and it has become difficult to enforce standards of behavior in public spaces, money has come to play a key role in two ways.
Traditionally in American culture, kids left home early. This goes along in part with our entrepreneurial, go-getter spirit.
